tier1.text: Intestinal villus goblet cells make mucus, a thick, slippery substance that keeps tissues moist. These cells release the mucus, along with fluid, into the hollow space inside the gut. These goblet cells sit in the surface layer of the villi, projections of the small intestine's lining. Each goblet cell is a one-cell gland tucked between column-shaped cells.

tier2.text: Intestinal villus goblet cells secrete mucus, a thick, slippery substance that keeps tissues moist and acts as a lubricant. The goblet cells release this mucus, together with fluid, into the lumen, the open space inside the digestive tract. A goblet cell is a gland made of just one cell; a gland is a structure of one or more cells that make and release chemical substances. In the small intestine, goblet cells are found in the mucous membrane, a lining covered by protective mucus. Intestinal villus goblet cells are part of the cell layer covering each villus, a projection of the small intestine's lining. This covering layer is a simple columnar epithelium, a single layer of column-like cells, with goblet cells scattered through it.
